query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: During high-temperature exposure, degradation in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is governed by the quality of the oxide scale formed on its fcc matrix. In oxidizing atmospheres, rapid formation of a continuous and adherent Cr- and Al-enriched oxide layer suppresses further oxidation, whereas in reducing atmospheres the incomplete oxidation leads to formation of non-protective or even volatile Ti-rich oxides that compromise scale integrity and promote degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy possessing a continuous fcc matrix and a microstructure optimized for strength and fatigue resistance.
generation.intervention: Expose identical alloy samples to controlled high-temperature environments under (a) oxidizing conditions (e.g., air or oxygen-rich atmosphere) and (b) reducing conditions (e.g., hydrogen-diluted or low oxygen partial pressure gas mixtures).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–1000 °C) where oxidation kinetics are active, under well-defined oxygen partial pressures corresponding to oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, composition, and integrity of the surface oxide scale (notably the Cr- and Al-rich oxide versus Ti-rich oxide phases) mediate the overall degradation mechanism.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing conditions, the rapid growth of a protective and adherent oxide scale containing Cr and Al acts as a barrier to further oxidation. In reducing conditions, the dearth of oxygen prevents full formation of the protective scale; instead, localized formation of less adherent or volatile Ti-rich oxides occurs, leading to compromised surface integrity and subsequent degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, the alloy exhibits slower degradation rates (measured as minimal weight gain and retention of mechanical properties) due to a stable protective scale. Under reducing conditions, the alloy shows faster degradation (reflected in abnormal weight loss or non-protective scale formation, and microstructural evidence of subsurface attack) because of the unstable or volatile nature of the oxide products.
generation.baseline: Behavior of the as-manufactured alloy with its intact fcc microstructure prior to exposure; expected to have no pre-existing oxide scale artifacts.
generation.boundary: Findings are expected to hold in the specified high-temperature range (700–1000 °C) and within gas compositions that clearly define oxidizing versus reducing environments. Outside these boundaries (e.g., at much lower temperatures or ambiguous oxygen partial pressures) additional phenomena may interfere.
generation.uncertainty: While the central role of Cr and Al in forming protective oxides is supported by analogous studies in high-temperature alloys, the exact contribution and kinetics of Ti-rich oxide formation under reducing conditions in this specific composition remain less quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple identical samples of the alloy. Divide samples into two groups: one group is exposed to a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air or oxygen-rich gas) and the other to a reducing atmosphere (e.g., inert gas with a small fraction of hydrogen) at temperatures between 700–1000 °C for a fixed duration. Post-exposure, examine the surface oxide scale morphology, composition (using XRD, SEM-EDX), weight change, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity via cross-sectional SEM.
Composition analysis of the oxide scale using EDX or XPS (to confirm Cr/Al-rich versus Ti-rich phases).
Mechanical testing (e.g., hardness or tensile strength) to evaluate degradation of bulk properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exposed to oxidizing conditions do not exhibit a more continuous, protective Cr- and Al-rich oxide scale (and correspondingly better mechanical integrity) than those under reducing conditions—or if the reducing environment does not promote the formation of unstable/volatile Ti-rich oxides associated with degraded performance—the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
